title: Design the Supply Chain
intro: Three tasks, all of them calculations, and all three decide whether money gets spent. Keep a calculator or spreadsheet to hand. The figures are different from the ones worked in the video, deliberately — and each task contains one thing that is not in the headline numbers. Work each task before you look at the answers document.

sections.title: Task 1 · Net present value and discounted payback

blocks.text: NESR is considering an automated pipe-handling and inspection cell at a regional base. The equipment has a stated useful life of five years, after which it is expected to be fully written down with no residual value. The cost of capital is 12%.

answers.title: Task 1 · Net present value and discounted payback — worked

blocks.text: a)  The discounting table
b)  Total present value and net present value

items: Total present value of the inflows: 1,802,388.

blocks.text: c)  As a percentage of the investment

This is the whole task. The net present value is positive — so on the rule as normally stated, accept. But it is positive by one-eighth of one per cent of the investment. On a 1.8 million commitment the analysis has produced a margin of 2,388 dollars, which is less than the cost of the meeting that approves it.
d)  The two paybacks

head: Measure
Calculation
Result
rows: Discounted payback — cumulative PV after year 4

blocks.text: e)  The recommendation
Refuse, or send it back for better numbers. The correct one-sentence version:

"The net present value is positive by 2,388 on an investment of 1.8 million, and the discounted payback is 4.99 years against a stated five-year life — so on these figures the project breaks even three days before the asset is written off, and I cannot recommend committing capital on that margin without a firmer estimate of the annual cash inflow."
The assumption that flips it

items: The annual net cash inflow of 500,000. If it is 10% low — 450,000 — the total present value falls to about 1,622,000 and the net present value becomes roughly negative 178,000. If it is 10% high, the NPV rises to about 182,000. A ten per cent estimating error swings the answer by 360,000, which is 150 times the margin the analysis produced.
Note also that the discount rate does the same thing. At 14% rather than 12%, the same cash flows are worth about 1,716,000, and the NPV is negative.

blocks.text: The general lesson, and the reason this task exists. "NPV is positive, therefore accept" is a rule that only works when the NPV is comfortably positive. When it is marginal, the right response is not to approve or refuse on the number — it is to go back and reduce the uncertainty in the input that dominates it. A decision that a ten per cent estimating error would reverse has not actually been made by the analysis. It has been made by the estimate.
a)  The case as proposed: 12 variants down to 5
b)  Reworked for the technical note
Variant 7 cannot take the common part, so the consolidation is 12 → 6, not 12 → 5. Three things change.

head: Step
Calculation
Result
rows: Does it still clear the 25,000 tier?

blocks.text: c)  The gap, and the condition

items: 2.61 years against 2.40 years is a difference of 0.21 years, or about two and a half months.

The three things the footnote changed: 2,400 units a year keep paying the old price, so the purchase saving falls by 7,200; the pooling benefit is smaller because six part numbers pool less than five, so the carrying saving falls by about 1,479; and the engineering cost does NOT fall, because the work to qualify the common part is the same.

blocks.text: The commercial condition: the supplier's volume tier. The data says the supplier "has indicated" a tier at 25,000 units. Indicated is not agreed. The purchase saving is 82,800 of a 98,829 annual benefit — 84% of the case — and it exists only if that price is honoured at the consolidated quantity. Get it in writing, at the 27,600 figure rather than the 30,000 figure, before any part of the 210,000 engineering spend is committed.
What to do if the tier does not hold

items: Without the price reduction the annual benefit falls to 7,029 + 9,000 = 16,029, and the payback goes from 2.6 years to about 16 years. The project is not marginal at that point. It is dead.

Which is the real finding: this is not an engineering business case with a commercial input. It is a commercial business case with an engineering cost attached, and it should be presented in that order.

blocks.text: Two general lessons. First, one technical exception in a footnote moved the answer — and there is almost always a variant 7. Ask for the exceptions before you build the model, not after. Second, when one line is more than 80% of the benefit, the business case is really about that line, and everything else on the page is detail.
a)  The headline figures
On those figures, approve. For every dollar invested, 1.27 is returned.
b)  Tangible benefits only

This is the trap. On tangible benefits alone the ratio is BELOW 1.0 and the return is NEGATIVE. The project does not clear the bar on the money anybody can invoice — it clears it only because two estimated numbers, worth 220,000, were included. Those two lines are 26% of the benefits and 122% of the net gain.
c)  Annualised

items: 27.3% over four years annualises to 1.2727 to the power of one quarter, minus one — which is 6.2% a year.
Against a hurdle rate of 8% a year, it does NOT clear. And on tangible benefits alone it is negative, so it does not clear any hurdle rate at all.

blocks.text: d)  The recommendation
Do not refuse it — refusing it on these figures would be as lazy as approving it on the headline. The correct answer is a conditional recommendation:

"The proposal returns 1.27 for every 1.00 invested over four years, which annualises to 6.2% — below our 8% hurdle. And on tangible benefits alone the ratio is 0.94 and the return is negative 6.1%, so the case rests entirely on two estimated benefits worth 220,000. I would not approve it until (a) those two estimates are re-derived by consensus across operations, commercial and finance rather than by one function, and (b) the hardware line is re-priced, because RF infrastructure for a live warehouse is the line that is understated in almost every proposal of this kind."
The cost line to challenge, and why

items: Hardware — scanners and RF infrastructure at 110,000. This is a one-time project expense, and the source names exactly this category as the one that hides costs: fees to investigate alternatives, data conversion, and lost productivity during the learning curve. RF coverage surveys, cabling in a working warehouse, ruggedised devices and spares, and the device refresh that will fall inside a four-year window are all routinely omitted.

A defensible second challenge: internal resource time at 55,000 across four years is roughly a quarter of one full-time person. For a warehouse management system implementation with data cleansing and a live cutover, that is low — and the source is explicit that a salaried employee being a sunk cost does not mean the cost of reallocating them can be ignored.

blocks.text: And what is legitimately in the project's favour, because a good review says this too: the intangible benefits are real, not invented. Improved customer service from accurate inventory is exactly the sort of benefit the source says should be estimated by consensus rather than dropped. The problem is not that they were included. It is that they were included without the tangible-only figure being shown alongside — and that is what turns an honest case into a misleading one.
